maintopic: SIR JOHN A. MACDONALD ESTABLISHMENT OF LEGAL HOLIDAY IN MEMORY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in 1967 Canadians will be celebrating throughout Canada the birth of their nation. As Sir John A. Macdonald was the first prime minister of Canada, it seems proper and desirable that his memory should be honoured by the observance of a holiday in the name of Sir John A. Macdonald day.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a question to the Minister of Public Works. I apologize for not giving him sufficient notice, but I sent my question to the Postmaster General's department and it was redirected to him. My question is based on a copy of a letter I received from the municipal clerk of the corporation of the village of Kaslo, British Columbia, addressed to the Postmaster General, Ottawa, which says:
I have been directed to refer you to the promise made that a new post office was to be built in Kaslo during 1962.
I must bring to the attention of the house the fact that Kaslo is the birthplace of a very distinguished Canadian, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Green). The letter goes on to say:
It has now been ascertained that this project is not to be undertaken.
In view of the inadequacy of the present post office for the public of Kaslo and district the board of commissioners and public generally urgently request that this matter be reconsidered and that arrangements be made for a new post office to be built without delay.
My question is this. In view of the great need for a post office and the particular circumstances surrounding this village, will the minister reconsider his decision?

speakeroldname: Hon. D. J. Walker (Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
subtopic: KASLO, B.C.  REQUEST FOR NEW POST OFFICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I did not realize until this moment the great importance of Kaslo. I think perhaps this matter should be drawn to the attention of the historic sites and monuments board. After all, there is no one in Canada, other than the Prime Minister, who is more famous than the Secretary of State for External Affairs.
I assure the house that this matter is engaging our earnest attention even without having known the important significance of Kaslo, and we will be building a new post office there in the next year. In the meantime, however, we have an unexpired lease and adequate quarters at a low rental. I assure the hon. member for Kootenay West that when the post office is built we will endeavour to persuade the Secretary of State for External Affairs to assist my hon. friend in opening the building.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: CUBA-REPORTED STATEMENT BY U.S. SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: I have a question to direct to the Prime Minister. Has he any comment to make on the Washington report of a statement by United States Secretary of State Dean Rusk with regard to an appeal to O.A.S. member states concerning a cessation of trade with Cuba?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
maintopic: CUBA-REPORTED STATEMENT BY U.S. SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
I had expected that question would be asked, Mr. Speaker. I would point out that the Leader of the Opposition asked a similar question the other day. That was, of course, prior to the statement made by Mr. Rusk; hence the anticipation with which I looked forward to the opportunity of answering this question.
We have no official reports on the conclusions reached by the foreign ministers of the organization of American states at the Punta del Este conference. I am, however, not aware of any decision taken by that meeting which relates to restrictions on trade with Cuba in non-strategic materials and goods.
In so far as the export of arms to Cuba is concerned, as the house has been informed on
480	HOUSE OF
Inquiries of the Ministry a number of occasions the Canadian government has not been permitting the export of arms to that area for more than two years, and in addition has not been allowing the export of strategic materials to Cuba.
In the statement appearing in the press, reference was made to the suggestion that the earnings by Cuba on her exports to Canada might be used "to promote communist subversion in neighbouring countries". I would point out that Canada's trade with Cuba in non-strategic goods runs heavily in favour of Canada, and that therefore there can be no possibility of earnings by Cuba on her exports to Canada being used for this purpose. On the contrary, Cuban trade with Canada is absorbing dollars secured from other sources.
I think it might be of interest in that connection to point out the record for the first nine months of 1961 with regard to both exports and imports. Canada's exports to Cuba amounted to $21.5 million. Imports from Cuba amounted to $4.6 million. During the same period United States exports, while they were tremendously down from those of the previous year, amounted to $13.3 million and imports to $26.8 million.
With regard to the problem in general may I say this. While naturally Canada is most desirous of co-operating at all times with friendly nations, the decision as to the course Canada shall take should be made by Canada on the basis of policies which we believe are appropriate to Canada.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of Ihe Opposition):
maintopic: CUBA-REPORTED STATEMENT BY U.S. SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: May I ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce what are the actual steps that are taken to ensure that goods exported from the United States to Canada are not then re-exported from Canada to Cuba?

speakeroldname: Hon. George H. Hees (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
maintopic: CUBA-REPORTED STATEMENT BY U.S. SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Exporters of goods to Cuba are required to declare what goods are contained in the shipments. If anything which comes from the United States is attempted to be shipped to Cuba, that shipment is refused. That has happened on a number of occasions. We are watching this matter very closely. I do not believe there has been a single instance in which goods which originated in the United States have been shipped to Cuba.

maintopic: CUBA-REPORTED STATEMENT BY U.S. SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: I thank the minister for his answer. May I ask him this question. What steps are taken to ensure that goods exported from Canada are not originally from the United States? Are the exporters asked to give the original source of the goods exported to Cuba?

I believe they are asked to do that, Mr. Speaker. However, I should like to


get information on the exact procedure, because I do not wish to make a misleading statement in the house. I will produce it early next week.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister; Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, before the house adjourned yesterday evening, I had quoted a few figures to show how efficient the winter works program was. I should like to complete the information I gave by adding, for example, that during the winter of 1960-61, in the St. Hyacinthe district, ten municipalities participated in this program. The work done cost $1,153,845, of which $144,156 were paid in salaries, and it provided jobs to 413 workers.
During the winter of 1959-60 in the city of St. Hyacinthe alone, according to the report published by the board established to promote winter works, a sum of $126,935 was spent on such projects and 118 men were employed. As indicated in the report, the figures were incomplete, owing to the fact that many contractors had yet to report.
I think it is only fair to say that the municipalities would have availed themselves of this program long before that, had the opposition
Supply-Labour
not raised a hue and cry against it, spreading fear and panic among the municipalities.
During the year 1958-59, according to the figures now available, 41,500 workers, throughout Canada, and 647 municipalities have been assisted by the winter works program introduced by the minister. In 1959-60, 51,600 workers received wages produced by those projects undertaken by 869 municipalities.
Finally, during 1961-62, it is estimated that the projects submitted to the government by 2,286 municipalities will provide employment for 111,200 workers. Man days provided as a result of that program will add up to 4,743,000.
According to hon. members of the opposition, this program is not worth paying attention to and the municipalities should almost be blamed for participating.
In their speeches, the hon. members of the opposition have made a survey of the situation. I should also like to discuss the situation in the province of Quebec and compare it with what it was when our hon. friends the Liberals were running this country.
But before doing that, Mr. Chairman, I should like to call your attention to an article by Pierre Charbonneau in Le Nouveau Journal on November 30, 1961. I quote:
Plank number 12 of the Quebec Liberal party platform reads as follows: ''The provincial government must assume its responsibilities with regard to unemployment."
I read a little further on:
In short, it emerges clearly from that analysis- and the speeches made by Mr. Lesage and his colleagues during the electoral campaign of June 1960 have confirmed it-that unemployment is primarily the responsibility of the province.
And still further on:
Although sympathetic to the cause of the unemployed, Quebec admits its helplessness and passes the buck to Ottawa, satisfied to play a purely supplementary part. What about the council for economic guidance? And what about the pursuit of "the necessary policies" mentioned in the Liberal platform?
At this point, I would like to refer to an advertisement published, in 1960, by the Liberal party during that campaign. It states:
The Liberal solution to the unemployment problem is as follows: 1. consider unemployment as a family problem and a provincial responsibility.
Now, Mr. Chairman, for the information of the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rose-mont (Mr. Deschatelets) let us now compare

Supply-Labour
the percentage of unemployed under the administration which preceded that "terrific team" in Quebec.
When the said "terrific team" took over in Quebec, the percentage of the jobless in the province was 5.7 per cent. In July 1960, that percentage rose to 6.5 per cent, and reached 6.2 per cent in August, 6.4 in September, 6.9 per cent in October, 7.9 per cent in November and 10.1 per cent in December.
Moreover, in March 1961, when the Quebec Liberal government was claiming to have done something to keep unemployment down, the percentage of people without work in that province went up to 15 per cent as against 13 per cent at the same time a year before.
The damage was terrific.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister; Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext:
Those figures are taken from the publication sent to us by the dominion bureau of statistics, and I would like my friends opposite to make more frequent use of it in their speeches.
We also heard from the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont that there was full employment, under the former government. I would like to refer my hon. friend to the years 1937, 1938 and 1939, when a Liberal government was at the helm, and there were about 400,000 unemployed, a large number of them on relief. And 400,000 unemployed, at that time was a much higher proportion, since the labour force was then much smaller than it is now.
However, during the years 1937, 1938 and 1939-years of plenty according to our hon. friends opposite-in the city of Montreal and in other large cities across Canada, there were doctors, notaries, lawyers, nurses and teachers on relief. These people were receiving direct assistance. However, our hon. friends opposite now would have us believe that there was full employment at that time.
Our hon. friends will also recall that in those years, wages of 10, 12 and 15 cents per hour were being paid in the textile industry, and when you compare average salaries then and now in that industry, you cannot but recognize that Canadian workers, under the present Conservative regime, are far better off now than ever before.
In fact, it cannot be contended that we are living under a hunger regime when Canadians earn more, spend more and save more.

It must also be remembered that there are more Canadians at work today than ever before in Canada's history.
In the textile industry, for instance, the average weekly salary as of November 1956, was $55.96, while it reached $63.51 in November 1960.
In the manufacturing industry as a whole, the worker was earning $68.78 a week in November 1956 and $79.16 in November 1960.
In the building industry the average weekly pay was $70.78 in November 1956 as compared to $81.46 in November 1960. And I believe this last average has gone up since November 1960.
In the field of construction, according to a report by the secretary of the builders' association, Canada has established a world record.
In fact, Mr. John Caulfield Smith, executive vice president of the national association of house builders of Toronto, stated:
Construction accounts for 10 per cent of our gross national product as compared to 11 per cent in the United States and 8 per cent in Britain.
And since our friends opposite like to make comparisons with present full employment in England, Germany and Italy, does that imply that the Liberal policy would be to go back to longer hours and lower wages than those paid here? Do they intend to achieve full employment by reducing the wages and increasing the working hours of Canadian workers?
I feel that if the question was put to the Canadian worker, he would not hesitate to answer that the conditions which he enjoys now under a Conservative administration are indeed the conditions he prefers.
Mention was also made of certain Gallup polls. I should also like to draw the attention of this house to the results of a poll reported in the newspaper La Presse on January 4, 1962. The question put to people in various walks of life was as follows:
Do you approve or disapprove of the record of the federal government to date?
For the whole of Canada, the answer was as follows: for, that is favourable, 43 per cent. Against, 28 per cent, while 29 per cent of the population did not answer.

As far as the province of Quebec is concerned, the proportion in favour shows that this government did a very good job: 44 per cent were in favour; 29 per cent were against and 27 per cent did not answer.
Concerning the textile industry which is of particular interest to me, I should like to draw the attention of the house to information I have here.
I am quoting here from an article published in the Gazette of January 13, 1962, which is based on the publication entitled The Primary Textile Institute, with the following subtitle:	.

Textiles may enter new phase-obtain 51 per cent of domestic market-first increase since 1950.
Further on we read:
Industry optimism stems from a number of 1961 indications, such as an increase in domestic production, a levelling of the volume of imports, and the arrest of annual cuts in employment.
Further on we see:
Despite the difficult conditions since 1950-
Mr. Chairman, you will remember that hon. members opposite have tried to persuade us that the textile industry has only been in trouble since our government came into power; but you will note, sir, that this industry has been in trouble since 1950, and for the first time since that year is beginning to pick up. I was quoting this article:
Despite the difficult conditions since 1950. this industry has never ceased believing that it had a vital role to fill in the Canadian economy and the future of this country.
This is quite a bit different from what our Liberal opponents have been trying to persuade people all across Canada. (Translation):

He asked me to give figures and I am quite willing to quote some from memory.
In Canada-

September 1961.
I see.

When the results of the next Gallup poll are known, they will no doubt be even less favourable to the Conservative government.
For the information of the hon. member for Chambly-Rouville, according to the figures, the Liberal party's popularity was 56 per cent, while that of the Conservative party was 48 per cent.
Keep your present leader for a while and we will easily be returned to office.

An upturn in the textile industry was also mentioned. It was stated that employment had improved in that industry since the beginning of 1961. However, the situation is not quite as good as in 1956 when the Liberals left office. The Canadian producers' share of the domestic market was 56 per cent that year as compared with 48 per cent at the end of 1960. It has decreased continuously. If there is an improvement in the textile industry today, it is because there has been a marked improvement in the economic situation in the United States, and because the Americans are selling their products in their own country where the demand is heavy, which eliminates dumping in Canada.
I revert to the question of unemployment to enlighten the hon. member for St. Hya-cinthe-Bagot who claimed that the government's policy has reduced unemployment in the country and in his riding, in particular. I would suggest that he refer to the following figures which I find in the November issue of the Labour Gazette:
Employment opportunities and applications at the unemployment insurance commission as of September 29, 1961.
I must tell the hon. member that according to the above mentioned survey, by August 31, 1961, there were still 1,049 unemployed in the city of St. Hyacinthe. Yet, there are some who claim that the municipal winter works program helped alleviate unemployment.
Mr. Chairman, the government's policy in that respect certainly has some advantages, since it will help to provide work for 118,000 people over a period of 45 days. We do not criticize that policy; we merely hope that the government will improve it. The aims of the Minister of Labour are sound and appropriate, but the means considered to check unemploy-26207-1-32
Supply-Labour
ment are inadequate because they do not meet the wishes expressed by the population, the municipalities and the unemployed.
Do not insult Mr. Lesage.

I shall come back later on, if I may, to Mr. Lesage, since I have been driven to speak about him.
As far as winter works are concerned, it has been determined that materials represent from 66 to 68 per cent of the cost and labour, from 30 to 34 per cent. Of this last percentage, the federal government pays half. Fortunately, in certain provinces, a percentage of the labour cost is added. The Quebec government pays 40 per cent of the labour costs. Both the federal government and the Quebec government are to be congratulated for that.
The fact does remain, however, that municipalities have to pay from 68 to 72 per cent of the cost of materials, which this year is estimated at $267 million. Furthermore, municipalities have to pay an 11 per cent tax on those materials. Now, we are told that this year the federal government will spend about $33 million. Then, taking into account the tax to be levied by the federal government on these $267 million worth of materials, we find that it will receive $28 million. This goes to show how insignificant the federal contribution is. It amounts to just a few million dollars.
What we want, and what the municipalities' union and various other organizations have been asking, is that the government do more than it has done in the past by creating a fund from which municipalities could borrow at a reasonable rate. For pity's sake, let us do away with the 11 per cent tax on materials which municipalities buy for winter works.
These are suggestions we are making to the Minister of Labour, not to be nasty, but to help him deal with the unemployment problem, since we know that there were 413,000 unemployed in December and there are perhaps over 500,000 at the present time.
Last winter, the number of unemployed reached 713,000, and if means are not taken to improve the situation, we will have this same number again this year.
We made plenty of suggestions during the great debate on unemployment which took place in 1959. The Liberal party set forth 25 of them and I think that was enough to work out a solution which should alleviate the unemployment situation.

Supply-Labour
Since the hon. members from Quebec want details, I am prepared to give them some. We know that in 1959-60, the province of Quebec held the record for unemployment. It was the province which had the most unemployed in relation to its labour force. But by mid-December 1961, the province had dropped down to third place, thanks to the wise policy of premier Lesage who had then been in power only 18 months.
What has he done?

Although he took over from an administration which had turned everything upside down for 16 years, only 18 months after he was elected as leader of the government of the province of Quebec, Mr. Lesage had taken such measures that the province dropped to third place as regards unemployment. And I ask all the hon. members from the province of Quebec to examine the figures as they are published each month so that they may realize what Quebec can do when it has a fair and sound government.
Twenty two new taxes under the Lesage administration.
Under the Union Nationale government, the assistance provided to municipalities under the program amounted to nothing. Today the government pays 40 per cent of the cost of labour.
Who signed the federal-provincial agreement on unemployment insurance?

Mr. Chairman, during last year's debate I offered a few suggestions and I had one about profit sharing. I explained that under that formula, the worker shares in the profits of our business concerns, which helps to reduce production costs so that our products are in a better position to compete with those of other nations on the export markets. I found that the best way to do so was to bring about better co-operation in labour-management relations. That is why I asked the government and the Minister of Labour to encourage employers and employees to sit down together and discuss their problems rather than have each side pulling on the blanket and increasing difficulties.
The Minister of Labour has made no comment about my suggestions and the same goes for the unions. They had no comments to offer, except for one union leader who has expressed views I cannot give you here for the time being.

However, a fortunate movement was initiated recently by industrial leaders and management associations that met for the first time in Winnipeg recently. We are told that other meetings will follow in various parts of the country; I hope they will be successful in improving management-labour relations and will find ways to improve employment conditions throughout the country, which is something the government cannot do.
Mr. Chairman, I thought I should make an appeal in favour of the 400,000 people who were out of work in December and I have been sincere in this.
It is said that an amount of $33 million will be spent during the year in an effort to ease unemployment. That is not enough. If hundreds of millions are spent on war material that will probably never be of any use to us, I think that the $33 million that will be spent this year to fight unemployment are not enough. As the hon. member for Maison-neuve-Rosemont (Mr. Deschatelets) was saying yesterday, in wartime, there is a lot of money for armaments, whereas with a human problem like unemployment, the purse strings are tightened and nothing is done to solve it.
It is not by going back to the regime that prevailed in the years 1930-35 that the unemployment problem can be solved, but rather by examining it today in an objective manner and by working together to find a satisfactory solution. Unemployment is no more the responsibility of the provincial government than of the federal government or of the unions or of management. It is a problem which concerns each and everyone of us, a problem which concerns the government as much as each and every member of this house. It is not by indulging in bigotry, as has been the case yesterday and this morning, that a solution will be found to this problem of unemployment.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Hon. members will recall that during the throne speech debate I mentioned optimistically the employment situation in the Saint John area. This optimism was fortified the other day, namely on January 30, by a press report. I am quoting from the Saint John Telegraph-Journal.
Unemployment in Saint John at the end of 1961 showed a sharp decrease over the previous year, said Mayes C. Smith, manager of the national employment service office, yesterday.

I referred, however, to the increasing demands in our area for skilled labour. I mentioned the fact that the industries now located there were forced to go to the United Kingdom for their skilled people and that these immigrants are now moving into this part of New Brunswick. At that time I expressed the hope that it would be possible to increase our technological training facilities there so that it would not be necessary to bring in so many immigrants and we could make use of the fine young men who are now in Saint John.
This matter of increased vocational training has been to the fore in the last two or three weeks. A great many statements made at the various levels of responsibility have appeared in the press. I had hoped that it would be possible to make more progress than that which has been made. I am not suggesting that any of the statements that have been made are untrue. However, I make mention of this fact because I think the impression could have been created in some minds that the nigger in the woodpile is the federal government. Some of the figures that have been used, while not untrue, create the wrong impression.
I should like to take the example of a proposed expenditure of $1 million on construction for vocational training. Under the plan made possible by the Technical and Vocational Training Assistance Act of last year and the agreement thereunder the federal government would match 75 per cent of all money paid by the provincial government. The provincial government of New Brunswick is hamstrung owing to an old and outmoded vocational education act and can assist only to the extent of 30 per cent. This would mean that 25 per cent of the 30 per cent, which would be paid by the province, would amount to only $75,000, which is a paltry sum indeed. Suppose the provinces paid the full $1 million for this proposed construction. In that event the province would receive back from the federal government $750,000. This would leave only $250,000 as the net amount to be paid by the provincial government. However, the provincial government are welshing on this because they would only pay $75,000 under the existing scheme and would therefore save themselves $175,000. This has the effect of making it impossible for the municipality to go ahead with its plan. I understand that in the Saint John case the estimated cost is $500,000 and if we take half this amount this means that the provincial government by hiding behind this 26207-1-32*
Supply-Labour
outmoded act is saving approximately $80,000, or half of $175,000. As a result we will not be able to go forward with this very necessary construction to provide facilities for training people in the skills that are necessary in the Saint John area.
I suggest that when the provincial act was drafted the circumstances were entirely different. Revisions have been made with regard to the federal responsibility, and it is up to the province now to make the necessery changes so that we will all be able to benefit from this very generous offer of which advantage has been taken by most of the other provinces.

Mr. Chairman, my remarks will be brief because there is no need now to answer the statements of the opposition. I think the Minister of Labour did so very effectively last night when he outlined just how much good this program is doing all across Canada. On the radio this morning I heard complimentary remarks by a commentator about this program of the government. The commentator said that the opposition had fired no big guns against the program. He implied that they had let off a few firecrackers, and I think he believed that even among those firecrackers there were quite a few duds. In my opinion the opposition has endorsed this program by praising it with very faint criticism.
The two items now before the committee are very important. Item 613 provides an amount of $90,000 for the promotion of a program to combat seasonal unemployment. The Minister of Labour expressed his appreciation of the work of the local winter works committees and their great efforts in providing more jobs during the winter. I should like to add my personal commendation to the minister's letter of thanks which he addressed last year to the local winter works committees. May I say with particular reference to the Moose Jaw winter works committee that I think their efforts will certainly deserve thanks from the minister again this year.
During the debate on acreage payments I drew attention to the fact that the item covering those payments to western farmers and the item of $40 million for winter works appeared on the same supplementary estimate sheet. I said at that time that the $42 million in acreage payments will help to bolster the income of the western farmers and the $40 million in item 614 now before us, the purpose of which is to pay half the labour costs for winter works, will add to the income of the workers. I repeat what I said in the earlier debate. The fact that the two items appear on the same supplementary
And the fact that there may be an election on April 9 may have something to do with it.

The minister referred to the scope of the program last winter. This list of claims is only one cheque requisition. This requisition is two pages long, and it shows the money paid from Ottawa to the provincial government and to the municipalities. There are quite a few of them in my own constituency but I shall not read the items.
What about the minister's own riding?

This list of claims processed for payment by Ottawa is covered by just one cheque requisition for $99,246, and I am sure it is only one of hundreds of such requisitions. After the projects are accepted, in my particular area anyway, Ottawa pays the money to the provincial government at Regina which in turn pays it to the municipalities. I do not doubt that the provincial government takes a great deal of credit for that, but I want to make it very clear that we are paying half the labour costs, as can be seen by this item for $40 million.
In my files I have letters of thanks for the part I played in some of the major municipal projects, and I pass on these expressions of thanks to the minister who is doing so much to provide jobs during the wintertime and thus reduce seasonal unemployment. The government programs implemented in the past four years have provided another benefit not directly connected with these payments from the federal treasury. This benefit is connected with winter construction. In earlier years it was taken for granted that construction work could not be carried out during our cold winters, but the example set by the winter works program has been followed by contractors all across Canada, as can be seen by the buildings now rising in Ottawa. Only this morning I passed a nine storey building on which work was being carried out in 19 below zero weather.
This is another part of the government's campaign to provide more employment, a campaign for which the Minister of Labour can take a great deal of credit. On behalf of my constituency, which has benefited considerably under this winter works program and which will benefit to an even greater extent this winter, I am happy to support this supplementary estimate, and I thank the minister for introducing it so early this session. province of Quebec was headed by Mr. Duplessis who did not want to contribute anything to such a program. But, today, the provincial government has realized that the responsibility for unemployment is not exclusively a federal one. The provincial governments, as well as the municipalities and all Canadian citizens must realize that this is a joint responsibility. When each of us accepts his full responsibility in this field, then, and only then, shall we find the real answer to our unemployment problem in Canada.

I would have a suggestion for the government in connection with the winter works program, as we all believe that there always will be some seasons in this country when the number of available jobs will not be large enough to absorb all our workers, more especially during the winter months. The very fact that 22 municipalities undertook winter works last year and that there will be this year a still greater number taking part jointly in the winter works program to help the unemployed indicates that the winter works program has been of assistance to them. I also believe that the municipalities could benefit more from these joint projects if they could find the money that is needed to undertake certain municipal works at a lower interest rate.
As you know, Mr. Chairman, the problem now facing many municipalities wishing to undertake these works is to find the required capital at a reasonable rate.

Mr. Chairman, while the government and its supporters persist in creating the impression that the opposition, while approving the supplementary estimates, are against winter works, I believe that they should rather realize, in all fairness, that the opposition is trying to convince the government that the responsibilities of unemployment, shared by the provinces, by the federal government, and up to a certain point by the municipalities, should be supported by all three levels of government.
However, one thing remains: it was not the provincial governments, nor the municipalities who, in 1957 and in 1958, promised to cope with unemployment and1 that nobody would ever suffer from unemployment in this country.
It was the present Prime Minister himself who, during his 1957-58 election campaign, stated that no Canadian would have to suffer from unemployment.
You will admit, Mr. Chairman-and all members on the government side will also admit-that in the political speeches made at that time there was no mention of asking the provinces or the municipalities to pay for most of the costs of winter works. The promise made by the Prime Minister during the 1957-58 election campagn was that of a political party who, today, is trying to fulfil only part of that promise and pass responsibilities on to municipalities and provincial governments.
You hear members on government benches boasting that the government is paying 50 per cent of the costs of those projects. We, on this side of the house, admit that the plan suggested by the federal government is probably a good one but we believe that it is inadequate to cope with unemployment.
We say that it is unfair to ask the municipalities to bear in practice the biggest part of the cost.

First, it is well known that federal government contribution amounts to only 50 per cent of labour costs. Besides, we all agree that at the present time when mechanization is now well established in this country, so to speak, most of those jobs are done with mechanical equipment. Thus those winter works projects could be done more cheaply by municipalities in more favourable seasons. It also happens that municipalities have to spend considerable amounts of money in order to reduce unemployment.
I said a moment ago that the 1957 and 1958 promise was not made by the municipalities nor by the provincial governments.
How about those of 1950?

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
It seems strange to me that this government which certainly deserves some credit for the winter works program should try to take all the credit.
I say that hon. members on the government side should honestly recognize that, if it had not been for the co-operation of provincial governments and municipalities, the program would be a complete failure. I hope they will agree that provincial governments also share in this effort and that municipalities assume an extraordinary burden in order to help in the solution of the unemployment problem. Hon. members have very little to say about it because they seek to give all the credit to the federal government.
Well, I say, Mr. Chairman, that unemployment is a plague which the government should have tackled much sooner than it did. In fact, it was only in September 1960 that this government recognized unemployment as a national emergency which had to be faced.
Until then, the right hon. Prime Minister himself as well as all the other cabinet members were charging the opposition with spreading confusion throughout the country with their statements on unemployment. The government refused to recognize that the plight of the unemployed was critical and called for government intervention.
It so happened that in September, 1961 the Prime Minister became aware of the feelings throughout Canada on that matter, and finally agreed, in a television program, that a serious unemployment problem had developed in Canada and that in such circumstances the government had to call an earlier session in order to settle the matter. Once again, a winter works program which had already been applied for a few years but in which the province of Quebec, for one, did not want to partake was proposed at that session as a corrective measure.
I am very much surprised now to hear some Conservative members from Quebec

offer fulsome praise to this government for its winter works program. You will admit, Mr. Chairman, that those same Conservative members from the province of Quebec would do well, once in a while, to thank the present government of the province of Quebec for having agreed to participate in those works.
