He should have said, rather, that it was a logical speech reminding the Conservative members from Quebec that the carrying out of this winter works program is possible in their province only because there is a Liberal government in Quebec.
To come back to the subject I was dealing with before one o'clock, I was referring to a request which had been made to the Minister of Labour by the northeastern Ontario municipalities association. I happen to have the text of that resolution here, and I shall read it to you as it is written, that is in English. I quote:
(Text):
That the winter works program be replaced by an assistance works program beginning one month prior to the present program and lasting one month longer and that grants for said program also cover equipment operators and supervisory staff.

(Translation):
This shows, Mr. Chairman, that the existing program even though it has its good points, is certainly inadequate in other respects and that the speeches of the members of the opposition are not made to oppose the winter works program, but rather to point out its flaws to the government and make suggestions which could easily be implemented.
Mr. Chairman, I was also saying before one o'clock that some government members from my province, namely the province of Quebec, seemed to give all the credit to the federal government. As far as I am concerned, I am willing to give this government the credit it deserves for its participation in this program. However, it would be sensible, I think, for government members from the province of Quebec, and from all the other provinces for that matter, to give some credit to the provinces and the municipalities.
For example, after reading an article published in Le Devoir of yesterday, I find that, this winter, the amount earmarked for winter works in the province of Quebec will total $81 million. Of that amount, thanks to an agreement reached by the provincial and federal authorities, the province of Quebec will pay $11,160,172 for labour costs whereas the federal government will pay $13,950,262. That clearly indicates that while the federal government is paying 50 per cent, the provincial government is paying 40 per cent. However, something else must be added: the municipalities will pay the sum of $3,286,576. That means that the total amount put up by the provincial government and the municipalities for the carrying out of such winter works in a province would be $14,446,000, compared to $13,950,000 put up by the federal government.
Therefore, in all fairness, a large share of the credit for that winter works program should go to the provincial governments and the municipalities. It must be noted, Mr. Chairman, that this total represents only the amounts paid in salaries. What about the cost of materials and machinery needed for carrying out the work? The provinces and municipalities must bear it alone.
In my opinion, that proves that there is a flaw in the winter works program.
The hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot (Mr. Ricard) stated yesterday that Liberal members seem unable to distinguish between the federal government's contribution of 50

per cent and that of the provincial government, which is 40 per cent. It is easy to work out the difference for someone who has reached the third grade level. It is a 10 per cent difference.
What the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot did not explain is the difference between 40 per cent and the Union Nationale's failure to contribute anything. That is a difference of 40 per cent. The hon. member did not work that out. No doubt he could have made the calculation, Mr. Chairman. He was able to do it, but he deemed it advisable not to do so.
Mr. Chairman, I have no intention of taking the 30 minutes I am allowed. I spoke for 12 minutes before one o'clock. I said certain things which deserve consideration. I shall continue along the same lines, since I shall now refer to the construction of technical schools.
I must tell the minister that a technical school is under construction in the community where I live. I wish to thank him on behalf of all my constituents. That project will certainly be most helpful to the people of the district.
That program was already in existence under the Liberal government, but the federal contribution has been somewhat increased, if my memory serves me right. However, we approved that measure to permit the construction of technical schools. What surprises me is that when the Liberal government was contributing to the technical school building program, the province which was refusing subsidies for winter works was also turning down grants for the construction of those schools.
The Quebec government refused federal assistance for the construction of technical schools for four or five years.
It is surprising to see that it was the government headed by the political leader of the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon)-Mr. Barrette's government-which was turning down the federal government's offer of financial assistance for the construction of technical schools.
Mr. Chairman, I rise on a point of order. The statements made by the hon. member just now are not true.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think that if an hon. member is not in agreement with what is said by the hon. member who has the floor, it would be better if he waited until the latter has finished his speech before answering back.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Besides, Mr. Chairman, I have only good feelings toward the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm. I had the occasion recently to make a trip in his
Supply-Labour
company and I learned to know him better. There is one thing, however, that I always find disappointing. In spite of all my efforts, he will not listen to reason.
(Text) :
Will the hon. member permit a question?

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
When I am through I shall be glad to do so. I can answer any questions the hon. member may ask.
(Translation):
On top of what the municipalities and the provinces have to pay.
I was blamed for quoting a political advertisement yesterday. I am going to quote another one, this time from the 1957 campaign. This one is more recent than the one I quoted the other day since that one dated back from 1956.
This advertisement refers to a Conservative candidate running in the province of Ontario, in a constituency next to mine. I quote:
(Text):
Do you wish to pay another further sales tax of 3 per cent to 5 per cent on everything you buy?
(Translation):
Now, the Liberals are being accused of playing off one province against the other. Well, I should like the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm to listen to this, and I quote the Daily Press of June 1, 1957:
(Text):
You shouldn't have to support municipalities in other provinces, when there is so much to be done in the Porcupine area. You should not be forced to pay additional sales tax, because the Liberal government refuses to give Ontario a fair share. You can raise your voice in protest.
(Translation):
Mr. Chairman, I believe the province of Ontario sent enough Conservative members to the house to indicate that it was protesting against the former administration.
The number of Conservative members in this house indicates that people did object, and that the program announced by the party in the federal election had a following. But the strange thing is that, today, we are paying a 3 per cent tax imposed by a Conservative government because it did not receive the $100 million it had been promised by the present Prime Minister of Canada.
Now, Mr. Chairman, municipalities contributing to winter works are paying the federal sales tax as well as the 3 per cent provincial tax.

Supply-Labour
That is the way, Mr. Chairman, in which this government fulfils the promises made in 1957-58.
Mr. Chairman, as I said before the house took recess, in a district like the one I represent, winter works are practically impossible.
There is one thing to which the hon. minister should pay particular attention, and that is the possibility of announcing his intention of sharing the cost of such works earlier in the season.
First of all, he will admit that, since the government took office, he has only announced in the late summer his intention of participating in such works during the year.
Now, municipalities have to prepare their budget in January, February, and sometimes in March. They are therefore quite unable to take any account of those winter works at that time. Therefore, even when the government announces its intention of continuing the winter works program, in July or August, municipalities can take no part in it because they cannot provide for this program in their budget.
The Minister of Labour, and the government, should tell us once and for all whether winter works will go on for a few years so that the municipalities can budget in order to take advantage of the program.
In closing my remarks, Mr. Chairman, I wish to mention again that a technical school is being built in my community and that the school board appreciates the assistance given both by the federal and the provincial governments.
We hope that this school will train young people to take up the challenge of life, or rather, I should say, the challenge of mechanisation we have nowadays.
I wish to thank the minister for the contribution his government has added to that we already had towards the construction of this building.
If my memory serves me right, Mr. Chairman, the former government was paying 50 per cent while the present government has raised this contribution to 75 per cent.
I wish to mention this, for, as I mentioned at the outset, I want to give credit where credit is due.
If the government, in order to fulfil a promise, has found a way to set up a winter works program, it has, on the other hand, burdened the municipalities and the provincial governments by making them share the cost of fulfilling this promise made by the present Prime Minister who had not, however, sought the permission of the municipalities or of the provinces.

Such is not always the case.
(Text):

The hon. member said he would reply to questions at the conclusion of his remarks. Having in mind that the Liberal party professes great concern about the unemployment problem and particularly the vocational training aspect of the over-all problem, would the hon. member explain why the Liberal government in the province of Quebec has only seen fit to participate in the over-all program of construction of vocational and technical training schools to the extent of $6 million whereas a Conservative government in the province of Ontario, which does more than profess interest, has participated to the extent of $139 million?

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: My answer will be given with pleasure. I simply say that the government of Ontario was able to benefit from the amount paid by the former administration to the extent of 50 per cent. Now they are taking advantage of the addition of 25 per cent more paid by the administration. In other words, Ontario was prepared for such a program so they could go into it more easily while on the other hand the province of Quebec refused for years to participate in the program. The fact is that the administration in Quebec was overburdened with debts incurred as a result of promises that had been made by a Tory administration.
The plan has been in effect for two years. What are you waiting for?

Mr. Chairman, last night the minister made a statement to the effect that the opposition had been critical of the action of the government in devaluing the Canadian dollar. I have not heard anyone on our side of the house make such a statement. As a matter of record, may I say that I for one have advocated the devaluation of the dollar for the past two years as a measure to stimulate exports and discourage Canadians from buying abroad. I know of no member of the official opposition ever having made a speech against the devaluation of the Canadian dollar. I should like to hear the minister say who made such statements and where they are alleged to have been made.
It was agreed that the two items under consideration should be considered at the same time to facilitate debate without unnecessary repetition, but we have heard much repetition yesterday and this morning on both items which are very closely related and involve $90,000 for publicity for the do it now campaign and $40 million by way of contribution to the municipalities under the winter works program. The minister referred first to the item of $90,000 to be spent for publicity to promote the do it now campaign.

This program, sponsored by advisory employment boards to the unemployment insurance commission and aided by the regional employment commission managers throughout the country, began some years ago, and I agree with the minister that it is being supported as a desirable means of providing additional winter employment.
The lakehead unemployment advisory board has carried on a do it now winter works campaign since its inception and with considerable success. We are fortunate to have men and women capable and willing to serve on these boards without remuneration of any kind. They certainly deserve the appreciation not only of those for whom they are helping to create employment but of the communities and the government. They spend hours at every meeting, some of which I have attended, trying to find ways and means of alleviating the vicious disease of unemployment.
In yesterday's issue of the Globe and Mail there is a story from Fort William reporting the sad statement by the city welfare director that 800 persons are now on relief, the greatest number reported at any one time since the depression of the 1930's. The welfare officer is reported to have said that the figures now stand at the highest level since the department started to keep accurate statistics.
There is no question of our support for the voting of this money to help to provide winter works. The idea of a federally assisted municipal works program was first put forward by the federation of mayors and municipalities at a winter employment conference convened by the Minister of Labour in Ottawa on July 14 and 15, 1958. Subsequently the proposal was again advanced at an informal conference held in Ottawa from October 6 to 8, 1958, between the federal cabinet and representatives of the federation of mayors and municipalities. Shortly after the adjournment of the informal federal-municipal conference, the federal government announced the first federally assisted municipal winter works program.
Seasonal unemployment is a continuous problem which is more or less peculiar to Canada both in good times and in times of recession. We feel it more today than at any other time during the past decade simply because of the widespread unemployment in fields where, up to a few years ago, it was only of a temporary nature whereas now it has assumed proportions with which it is hard to cope. The special provision for a program to
Supply-Labour
combat seasonal unemployment by the introduction of an expanded municipal winter works incentive program is to be commended, and while it will not cure the hard core of unemployment it will certainly help to absorb a number of men from the ranks of the unemployed.
The minister also made a statement to the effect that the average labour content of all municipal works is about 35 per cent. I regret to inform the minister that I do not agree with his statement. Since the federal government pays only 50 per cent of the labour costs, the federal government's share of the total cost of municipal projects amounts to approximately 17 per cent. This means that the municipalities involved bear the major brunt of the expenses incurred in the municipal winter works program. The provinces which contribute 25 per cent of the labour costs-I say this for the benefit of the hon. member for York-Scarborough who has just left the chamber-are Alberta, British Columbia, Manitoba, Ontario, Prince Edward Island and Saskatchewan. The province of Quebec contributes 40 per cent and Manitoba's contribution is 50 per cent provided the persons employed under the scheme have been on unemployment relief for a continuous period of 90 days.
In order to make this winter works incentive program really effective the government should also provide assistance to meet the costs of material, such as steel in the construction of bridges. In short, what the municipalities want is the government to share in the cost of materials used in the winter works program. The Canadian federation of mayors and municipalities, and other municipal associations have, from time to time, passed resolutions urging the federal government to establish a municipal loan fund from which municipalities may borrow money at a low rate of interest to finance local improvements. The participation of the government in costs of materials used in winter works projects, and the establishment of a municipal loan fund would give the winter works scheme a real incentive which would more than double, probably treble, the number of projects which municipalities would be able to undertake.
The submission of the Canadian federation of mayors and municipalities, presented to the government on November 10, 1961, deals at one point with the municipal winter works program. I wish to quote a few paragraphs from that submission which I think should be put on the record. They read:
One major obstacle to fuller municipal participation is the lack of any provision for financial assistance toward the cost of materials. Another

Supply-Labour
obstacle is the very real difficulty some municipalities have in obtaining the money needed for capital undertakings and at reasonable interest rates. Still another difficulty is that it is not practicable for municipalities-although they are willing to reschedule their work requirements as much as possible to the winter season-to make a sharp division between the seasons.
Moreover, while unemployment varies seasonally -although the highest incidence is in the winter- there is a serious amount of unemployment in all seasons. The need is for an all-year employment program of municipal works, which would extend both into and beyond the winter season, with provision for the scheduling of as much as possible of such work to meet the peak periods of unemployment in the winter .. . there are strong and compelling reasons why all levels of government should participate in the costs of essential municipal works irrespective of the season of the year in which they are taken. And there are equally good reasons why government-assisted employment measures should be maintained on a year-round basis.
For these reasons, the federal government is requested to give consideration to the following proposals:
(1)	That federal loans be provided to municipalities for capital works programs at a favourable rate of interest-extending the practice now followed in the financing of sewage facilities.
(2)	That federal contributions to municipal works be extended throughout the year with the federal government contributing a proportionately greater share of the labour and material costs involved for such work undertaken during the winter months of the year. If this is not feasible, the time should be extended to permit completion of projects already commenced during the winter season.
(3)	That municipal works for which federal aid is available under other forms of assistance (e.g. railway grade crossings) be considered as allowable projects for federal-assisted municipal winter works programs.
(4)	That measures be taken to assure prompt interim payments of the federal government's share and early final settlement of all federal-assisted municipal works programs.
As matters now stand, communities which would like to go ahead with a program of local improvements, but feel they cannot afford the costs and high interest rates, are inclined to postpone construction indefinitely, or to do it in the summer when costs are normally lower. The elimination of sales tax on building materials would also be a help to stimulate and speed up the execution of municipal works.
Mr. George Mooney, executive director of the Canadian federation of mayors and municipalities, made a statement some time ago that municipal governments across Canada are operating in a financial strait-jacket, a statement with which I fully agree. He knows that there is no city in Canada, large or small, that is not up to its neck in debt. Municipalities cannot depend only on property taxation for revenue, and should participate in some form of federal assistance. The Prime Minister himself recognized the problem when, during the 1958 election campaign, he

promised that his government would set up the municipal loan fund to provide low interest loans to municipalities.
It is all very well to try and stimulate the municipalities to proceed with winter works projects. I am all in favour of it, yet the government is offering the municipalities a cart without a horse, or bricks without mortar.
Having served my city of Fort William as an alderman and mayor, my sympathies are naturally with the municipal authorities and their financial problems. Indeed I am sure that the Minister of Labour, who served his city of Oshawa in similar capacities, must feel the same way as I do. The success of the winter works incentive program can only be achieved if the federal government proceeds to establish a municipal loan fund and enlarge its contribution by assuming a portion of the costs of materials used in these winter projects.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Shall the resolution carry?
(Translation):

Mr. Chairman, I had no intention of taking part in this debate. So small is the gift being offered by the government to those who are now unemployed that I could not bring myself to attach much importance to it. But having heard some of my colleagues, the one from St. Hyacinthe-Bagot (Mr. Ricard) and the other from Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon), I feel it is my duty to challenge some of the statements they made and I am going to make certain remarks about the slight success being achieved today by the winter works program, as compared to the nil results obtained by this program which the government introduced in 1958 and which was also in force in 1959 and at the beginning of 1960, when our Conservative colleagues from the province of Quebec still had as friends close to the provincial government the members of the Union Nationale and, as leaders, first, Mr. Duplessis, then Mr. Sauve, then Mr. Barrette, then Mr. Prevost, who, one after the other, all refused to do anything whatsoever to add to the little that the present federal government was offering in the nature of assistance to the hundreds of thousands of unemployed.
I heard yesterday the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot give a long list of projects for this year. I think he mentioned five communities in his constituency and said that 206 unemployed were provided with jobs through that winter works program.
I submit, Mr. Chairman, that at a rate of 200 unemployed per constituency and sometimes less, it will certainly be a while before

all our unemployed are supplied with jobs and a good many hon. members will have to rise here and give us their list of winter works to prove that this winter works program supplies jobs for hundreds of thousands of unemployed, as the minister claims.
Some 200 people have now found jobs in the constituency of St. Hyacinthe-Bagot for two reasons: first, there is no Duplessis government in Quebec and the Lesage government assumes 40 per cent of the cost of the wages paid under the winter works program; second, if the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot can boast about having supplied jobs to 200 unemployed as a result of that legislation, it is because it was extended this year in line with the recommendations and suggestions put forward in this house since 1958 by the Liberal party, when this winter works program began.
The hon. member complained about the fact that Quebec was contributing only 40 per cent of the cost of wages, but that, as he said, some of his friends who previously did not contribute anything-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister; Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I rise on a point of order. I wish to correct the statement made by the hon. member for St. Denis (Mr. Denis) because I did not complain at all about the fact that the Quebec government contributed 40 per cent-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I feel that the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot should postpone his corrections to the end of the speech of the hon. member for St. Denis.

Mr. Chairman, I do not object at all to the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot trying to imitate the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm, but he should at least find some other means of doing so, because he is taking the floor much too often.
The hon. member for St. Denis is the biggest liability to this nation and, therefore, to the province of Quebec.

Mr. Chairman, you have just heard the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm, more zany than brainy.
And now to continue with my remarks I shall come back to the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm and his eloquent speech of yesterday.
As I was saying, the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot boasted that Ottawa was contributing much more than the Quebec government, that is 50 per cent against 40 per cent by Quebec.
Supply-Labour
And now, what must he say of the other provinces which contribute only 25 per cent?
I think it is the province of Quebec which contributes most to the winter works program, and the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot is not satisfied. Would he like things to be as they were in years gone by, when Mr. Duplessis and the Union Nationale were in power, while the city of St. Hya-cinthe, the city where he lives, had no project at all?
If 200 people are now working in his constituency, he certainly should thank the Liberal government in Quebec and its decision, and not the winter works program introduced by the Conservative party in Ottawa.
And now, coming back to my friend the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm, who spoke at length yesterday- I don't know whether he was speaking extemporaneously, or whether he was reading a speech, or quoting from a newspaper or whether he mistook one reading room for another-
If you don't know, shut up.
I don't know whether he mistook one parliament building for another, because he spoke of the provincial government all the time.
You are speaking of it yourself.

And in reading over his speech, I note that more than half of it is stuffed with long quotations. So, I am of the opinion that the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm is misusing the time of the house by using it as a reading room. And all this to say that the Union Nationale was much superior to the provincial Liberal party now in power, while those people of the Union Nationale were doing nothing to contribute to the winter works program.
I must remind the hon. member that since the Liberal party has been in power in Quebec, advantage has been taken of all joint programs that could provide jobs to unemployed people in the province of Quebec.
I shall list only a few, such as the construction of the trans-Canada highway and of access roads to forests.
If I am not mistaken, the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm was secretary to the Hon. Antonio Barrette. I do not know if he kept the correspondence or the files from him, but I do know that Messrs. Barrette and Duplessis were against Quebec's participation in the building of the trans-Canada highway.

Supply-Labour
Now, Mr. Chairman, you realize no doubt that the building of a trans-Canada highway provides employment.
You are aware also that all provinces except Quebec took advantage of the joint plan for the construction of the trans-Canada highway in order to give work to the unemployed.
You are not without knowing that the construction of access roads to forests provides jobs for the unemployed.
I know that the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm was against that and now that the provincial government has decided-
Quote me.

-to give work to those unemployed, to accept its share of the federal government's money, we hear the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm rise and claim that it is unfair, we see him convene the mayors-
That is not true.

-of his riding's parishes to protest because the trans-Canada highway does not run through the constituency of Joliette.
Can you hear those people who did not want the highway at the time complain because it does not run through the constituency now that it has already been decided that is should pass elsewhere.

Mr. Mongrain shares my
opinion.

I now come to the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot.
The trans-Canada highway goes through his constituency. But do you know what he says, he who was so opposed to the construction of the trans-Canada highway? Here is what he says: "Is it not a shame? The provincial government has decided to cut through our farm lands".
What a clown.

There is no way of getting along with these people. Either they object or, when things run smoothly in spite of them, they complain that things are not going according to their tastes.
Well, if they do not keep pace with progress, Mr. Chairman, I am very much afraid that progress will pass them by.
You sound like Seraphin.

And they are not the only ones.

Last year, the hon. member for Chapleau (Mr. Martel) boasted, in this house, that he had succeeded in getting three roads of access built in his constituency.
Here are those roads of access: Amos-Matagami, Chapais-DesMaraisville, Wacou-michi-Albanel. The hon. member for Chapleau boasted in this house that he had obtained the construction of those three roads, and I do not blame him for it. But you must know, Mr. Chairman, that I am sure those roads could have been built years ago. Why were they not? Because our hon. friends from the Conservative party were in power in Quebec. (Text):

Use your brains and put your
brakes on, the next time.
(Translation):

As far as the Amos-Matagami road is concerned I must explain that they made a last minute effort-probably knowing that they would not succeed and so, they could blame the federal members-to have the Amos-Matagami road built on a costsharing basis by the federal and the province but their request was turned down because the contract had been allocated without calling for tenders.
That is the reason why one member of the present Quebec cabinet refused to accede to the request of our friends of the Union Nationale. And now that the province of Quebec has a Liberal government, those three roads have been built thanks to Mr. Lesage's administration. Yet, those people are still not satisfied. Indeed, I wonder when they ever will be.
When you stop talking.

When will they be satisfied with the generosity of the Liberal party in the province of Quebec?
Old age assistance was even refused in that province, where unemployment was among the highest in this country.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister; Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: Old age assistance was not refused.
I am sorry, it was not old age assistance, but unemployment assistance that was refused.
This is because you do not rise often enough in the house; it is a lack of habit.

I thank the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm for reminding me. But now, he knows we are discussing unemployment assistance, and assistance to people without work who may not benefit

from unemployment insurance. Is he aware of it or not? Does he know, or does he not know that the unemployed who does not get unemployment insurance is worse off than the man who does? Does he realize that?
When the Union Nationale administration was in power, all assistance to the unemployed was refused. And what were its supporters doing all the time? They were distributing kick-backs to their "needy" relatives and friends while the "wealthy" unemployed were left to starve.
That is what I infer from the stand taken by the friends of the Union Nationale.
Members of the Union Nationale are close friends of the Conservative members from Quebec in the house, but I also know that some of them have disowned their former friends. But the fact remains that if those friends of the Union Nationale had not taken part in the last election campaign in Quebec in the manner we know, I wonder how many of them would be sitting in the house?
To show how a Liberal government has been beneficial to the province of Quebec as far as the winter works program is concerned-I am addressing myself now to the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Mont-calm-I will give some facts, not merely do some guesswork. I am not quoting newspapers; these are facts that you cannot deny.
Knowing how much my colleague from Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm likes to talk, familiar as I am with his ideas and his nervousness, being aware that he likes to interrupt without giving other members a chance to reply, that he has probably fooled some of his friends by not letting them speak, I will now give facts.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I would ask the hon. member to please address the Chair.

It is with pleasure that I address myself to a more intelligent person than the previous one.
In 1958-59, 649 Canadian municipalities took advantage of the federal government contributions. In the province of Quebec, under the Union Nationale regime, the figure stood at 82, while in Ontario there were 208 of them. In 1959-60, the results were the same, with about a hundred more for the whole of Canada, a little more in Quebec.
But comes 1960-61. In Quebec, 600 municipalities availed themselves of the winter works program. In 1961-62, this year, the number goes up to 875.
In 1958-59, 169 projects were carried out in the province of Quebec under the Union
Supply-Labour
Nationale government. In 1959-60, always under the same administration, there were 174. In 1960-61, under Mr. Lesage's Liberal government, 1,720 were carried out, and 1,854 projects were approved in 1961.
You can see, Mr. Chairman, how beneficial it is for the province of my hon. friend from Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm to have a Liberal regime. In 1958-59, the federal contribution amounted to practically nothing. In 1959-60, the federal contribution to the province of Quebec under the Conservative winter works program, totalled $1.9 million in cash.
I would remind the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm that in 196061, with a Liberal government in power in the province of Quebec, the federal contribution reached $13.3 million. In 1961-62, it will be $14 million.
You can see how things change when a Liberal government takes over from a Conservative government in Quebec. You can see what it means to our unemployed. At least, the money we paid in taxes to Ottawa has found its way back to us, while, under the Union Nationale regime, we had nothing to eat but sweet autonomy.
Do not worry. It will be the end of you at the next election.

Now there has been boasting here about improvement in the unemployment situation in the last months. Well, it is in the province of Quebec that the improvement is mostly felt. If that statement is untrue, Mr. Chairman, I would like the minister to refute it.
That is easy.

I know that the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm finds everything easy, especially when he gets away from the facts. Yesterday, I asked the Minister of Labour whether all improvements in the winter program were not the result of suggestions from the Liberal party.
As you know, Mr. Chairman, all those who rose on this side of the house have always complained that the winter works program was announced too late. The Liberals always complained that the period during which the work was to be carried out was too short. The Liberal members who spoke complained that the special work, the types of employment which would be offered were too limited. This can be found on practically every page of Hansard, in almost every speech.
Is it not true that this year, the program was announced earlier? Is it not true, also, that this year and last year, instead of beginning in December, the period during which

Supply-Labour
the projects could be carried out was extended to last from October 15 to the end of April? Furthermore, is it not correct, Mr. Chairman, that in 1961, the winter works program contained a greater variety of projects? And to prove that those are suggestions of the Liberal party, I shall quote what the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) said on February 12, 1960, as can be found on page 1018 of Hansard. This is what he said:
How is it possible to do any of the projects within the narrow field of this plan?
And a little further on, he said:
First the length of time has to be stretched out so that it can be used in the month of October and November and in March and April-
And still further on:
The projects themselves have to be broadened-
And he also complains, in the same speech, about the delay in announcing the program. I shall read almost textually, the letter written by the Minister of Labour to Mr. Lesage, in 1961-
You are quite confused there.

I am now quoting the letter of the Minister of Labour:
We have been satisfied with the success of this first joint program, but we believe that there would be a way of fighting more efficiently against winter unemployment by broadening out the projects comprised in the program.
This is almost word for word what the hon. member for Essex East stated on February 12, 1960. And, for 1961, may I quote again from the letter of the Minister of Labour to Mr. Lesage:
We have again broadened the scope of the program.
Why was the scope of the program not broadened at a time when there were more unemployed than there are today? Why leave people in need for years before deciding to yield to the reasonable suggestions made by the opposition, or by the mayors of the various municipalities, and the various newspapers which have been almost unanimous in complaining of the fact that the winter works program was arriving too late. The newspapers have been almost unanimous in advocating an extension of the period during which the works can be carried out.
I have before me a list of editorial headlines. This is what the newspapers had to say:
The unemployed are being laughed at.
These are the words of Alderman Matte, of Quebec city.
Unnecessary expenses are being planned for.
That is the opinion of Alderman Burns also of Quebec city. You contend to be making handouts to the unemployed, but do not forget that this contention is far from the

truth: the handouts to the unemployed are not being made by the present government, but rather by the municipalities, since they pay 85 per cent of the costs relating to winter works.
Mr. Filibotte of Quebec city states:
Government publicity paid for by municipalities.
And Mr. Dozois:
The misleading nature of the legislation.
The latter is a friend of the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm. Instead of practising distributive justice and giving to one's "needy friends", the "rich unemployed" receive nothing.
A rush improvisation. You wonder whether it is not a bluff.
That one was from the Citizen and dates from December, 1958.
Absolutely inadequate assistance.
That is from Mayor Foucher, of Shawinigan. Mayor Hamel, of Quebec city, voiced exactly the same opinion.
A palliative-
Said Professor Art Lerner, director of the department of economics at Sir George Williams University. When he was in Quebec, Mr. Paul Sauve, had a laugh at the winter works program.
Ottawa should be more generous.
This is from the joint committee on winter construction works.
A drop in the ocean; a monumental joke-
-asserted Mayor Foucher, of Shawinigan.
Inadequate help-
-stated Mayor Nadeau, of Sherbrooke.
The experience of 1958-59 has been useless.
To put all the municipalities on the same level, various areas of the country should have been zoned. Quebec, on account of the cold weather-
-said Mayor Boivin.
Mean and insufficient program.
A drop in the ocean of unemployment.
Burden for municipalities.
Mr. Starr's "peanuts".
I also wish to mention the title of an article, a comment by a friend of the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm, Mr. Clement Brown:
Short of the country's needs.
This is what Mr. Clement Brown said on December 14, 1959. And I could continue indefinitely the list of comments by reporters, economists and specialists who complained about the meanness of this project.
Mr. Lesage made certain suggestions since he took over.
Twenty two new taxes in Quebec.

I am in favour of taxes to supply jobs for our unemployed, and I do not mind telling the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomp-tion-Montcalm; I am in favour of an increase in taxes to supply bread to those who have none. But I am not in favour of tax increases such as were applied in the past by the Union Nationale for the kind of distributive justice that was practised then. I am in favour of giving bread and butter to the unemployed, but I am not in favour of getting relatives and friends "in the paint" as the Union Nationale did.
Mr. Lesage offered the federal government to pay part of the cost of the material and equipment. Has the Minister of Labour answered that offer? Does he remember that when Mr. Mackenzie King took over in 1935, in order to offset Mr. Bennett's shortcomings, he shared in an extensive program of public works across the country and that he paid half of the cost? The "bout-de-l'ile" bridge which is in the vicinity of Joliette riding was paid for by the government to alleviate unemployment. The Pie IX bridge was partly paid for by the federal treasury in order to help the unemployed who were put out of work by Mr. Bennett.
The more it changes, the more it remains the same.
This government offers to pay half of the wage costs of additional labour you have to hire under the winter works program. That does not include foremen, regular employees, civil servants, accountants, architects, engineers, etc., but only the additional labour. But this cannot apply only to labourers, since the projects eligible under the 1958-59 plan included only sewer projects and sidewalks. Street lighting has been added since and now, thanks to the Liberal party, certain municipal building projects were added. I rose to speak about that one or two years ago and I blamed the government for not including tradesmen in this winter works program. I asked the minister to include buildings and construction in the winter works so that tradesmen-carpenters, bricklayers and electricians could work. It is only today that this can be done, that some constructions are allowed. But it was in 1958 and 1959 that these projects should have been allowed under the winter works program, and not three years after it has been in operation; not when you claim that the number of unemployed is lower today than it was two years ago.

speechtext: Order. I regret to interrupt the hon. member but I must tell him that his time has expired.

I only have a few more words to say.
