Bill of Rights BILL OF RIGHTS

the second reading of Bill No. C-4 to amend the Canadian Bill of Rights.
He said: I only intend to detain the house very briefly on this bill. My reason for saying that is because I hope the bill will be passed through the remaining stages before six o'clock, as I do not believe there is anything contentious in it and it certainly represents the professed aspirations of all hon. members in all parts of the house.
I introduced a similar bill which only got as far as first reading last year. Otherwise I am sure it would have been passed at the last session and perhaps, in order to save time, I might read the explanation I gave at that time, and add a very few words to it. It will be found at page 7395 of Hansard for Monday, July 3, 1961, at which point I said:
Mr. Speaker, this bill is being introduced at the present time because I have recently had my attention drawn to the case of a naturalized Canadian citizen of German origin with a Canadian born wife and three Canadian born children who is obliged to live abroad by the nature of his employment as one of the greatest living authorities in his field. Unless the law is changed this Canadian citizen will be deprived of his citizenship under Section 18 of the citizenship act, though no similar penalty would attach to a natural born Canadian citizen in the same circumstances.
By way of parenthesis I should like to say a word of appreciation to the hon. lady, the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mrs. Fairclough), who has taken what I think is a very wise and also very generous view of this particular case. Also I hope that before the case has again to be dealt with on an ad hoc basis, the law will have been changed so that this form of procedure will no longer be necessary. To continue with what I said on the last occasion:
The effect of the bill, if passed, would be to place naturalized citizens on a basis of complete legal equality with natural born citizens of Canada. Since all parties in the house have at one time or another advocated equality of Canadian citizenship, and since the present law works an injustice against naturalized citizens, I would hope that the house might see fit to dispose of this bill favourably before the present session is concluded.
I echo that hope for the session of 1962 and trust we can do it more speedily than we did most things in the session of 1960-61. At that point I was interrupted by Mr. Speaker who felt I was beginning to advocate my bill instead of merely explaining it. I bowed to his ruling, but the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) asked me to give some further explanation, and I think I should read the exchange which followed. It is:

speakeroldname: Hon. E. D. Fulton (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: At the risk of lengthening the explanation, may I ask the hon. gentleman if there are any other purposes, effects or implications of the bill he proposes to introduce.

I had intended to add that I hoped the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, until this bill has been disposed of by parliament, would not deprive any Canadian of citizenship under section 18 of the act. That was all I had intended to add.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: And there are no other effects or implications?

I will not give a legal interpretation. The minister can do that himself.
Now sir, while I do not intend to give a legal interpretation even today, perhaps I should read the explanatory note to the bill so that it will be on the record of Hansard. It says:
The purpose of this bill is to guarantee, expressly and by inclusion in the Canadian Bill of Rights, that a Canadian citizen may only lose his Canadian citizenship by himself renouncing it: that no law of Canada, nor any person or authority acting under a law of Canada, may arbitrarily strip him of his Canadian citizenship. For greater certainty, the amendment provides that, in any law of Canada an express declaration under section 2(1) that such law operates outside the safeguards of the Canadian Bill of Rights cannot be used to erase this right of citizenship from the bill of rights.
Put very simply all this bill would do would be to say that once the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration has conferred citizenship, under the authority given by this parliament, on any person who was not previously a citizen of Canada, no one can strip that person of his citizenship at any time in the future except himself, and he can do it only by becoming the citizen of another country. Now I know that many arguments can be made-that is why the discrimination that exists in the present law is there-for taking away the citizenship that is given under the law, but is does seem to me that all those arguments, when you really examine them, are just as valid against Canadian born citizens.
One of the discriminations in the present existing law, and one that I do not think most of us would object to in itself, is that if a naturalized citizen goes out of Canada, is accused of a treasonable act and refuses to come back here to stand trial, he can be stripped of his citizenship. But if a Canadian born citizen goes outside Canada, is accused of a treasonable act and does not come back to stand trial, he cannot be stripped of his citizenship. It seems to me there should be the same law for one as for the other.
There should not be this discrimination but there is a much wider and important discrimination in the existing law. It is that any citizen who is naturalized and has spent 10 years out of the country without taking certain legal steps to preserve his citizenship

can have his citizenship cancelled. In saying that I hope the hon. lady, the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration will correct me if I am wrong, because every day it gets a day longer since I was last in charge of the department and my failing memory may have betrayed me.
There are a number of practical advantages to that provision in the law. I admit that at once. That is why it was put there when the Canadian Citizenship Act was first put on the statute books in 1946. However, as against the practical advantages it does seem to me there would be the great, over-riding advantage of being able to say to all these people who come of their own free will and accept citizenship in this country, "In giving you Canadian citizenship we are giving you exactly what Canadian born people have".
It is such an advantage to be able to say that as compared with these few rather administrative inconveniences that we should not balance the one against the other. I would be proud to say that all Canadian citizens are equal just as far as the law can make them equal. They are not now.
Let us all, in a non-partisan way, join together this afternoon and as far as this house is concerned do what is necessary between now and six o'clock to make that proud boast a part of the law of our country.

Mr. Speaker, it is indeed a very great pleasure for me to follow the hon. member for Bona-vista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) who has introduced Bill No. C-4. It is especially a pleasure because we share something in common, coming from the same part of Canada, although I might say that he is not the least of our exports from the province of Manitoba.
One of the greatest.

The bill in question and the remarks of the hon. member regarding it I think commend themselves to most hon. members of this house. I think all of us feel that once a person is granted a certificate of Canadian citizenship he should be accepted on the basis of equality before the law of Canada and should have the same privileges as any other Canadian citizen, whether he is a Canadian born or naturalized Canadian citizen.
The point that concerns me, however, is the manner in which this bill is being brought in; that is, as an amendment to the Canadian Bill of Rights. To me the Canadian Bill of Rights should be, and I think is, a general statement in which is enshrined the basic fundamental freedoms which we enjoy in this country. I do not think it should be
Bill of Rights
cluttered up with a number of different types of amendments which could be better dealt with under other statutes.
As I read Bill No. C-4 it sems to me it has particular reference to the citizenship act. As the hon. member who introduced this bill was the minister of citizenship and immigration in the former government, I wonder why this bill was not brought in as an amendment to the citizenship act. Except perhaps that he felt if it is brought in as an amendment to the bill of rights it will, of course, be on a much higher plane. However, at the same time I think it would detract a great deal from the precise language and the general statement contained in the bill of rights.
I should like an explanation about two phrases in this bill because I think they are rather vague. I should like to quote from the bill:
A Canadian citizen ceases to be a Canadian citizen only if he voluntarily renounces his Canadian citizenship by his formal declaration or by his acceptance of the nationality or citizenship of a country other than Canada:-
The phrase "by his acceptance" is certainly rather vague. There are instances where children of naturalized Canadians or born Canadians go with their parents to another country where their parents become citizens of that country and automatically under the law of that country the children become citizens. How can we, in this case, say this is a voluntary renunciation? That is another vague phrase which I find in this bill.
If this bill were passed as an amendment to the bill of rights it would affect several sections in the Canadian Citizenship Act. It appears to me as I glance through the act that sections 4 (2) and 5 (1) (a) would be affected. Perhaps I may read part of those sections. Section 4 (2) of the act reads:
A person who is a Canadian citizen under paragraph (b) of subsection one and was a minor on the first day of January, 1947, ceases to be a Canadian citizen upon the date of the expiration of three years after the day on which he attains the age of 21 years or on the first day of January, 1954, whichever is the later date, unless he
(a)	has his place of domicile in Canada at such date; or
(b)	has, before such date and after attaining the age of 21 years, filed, in accordance with the regulations, a declaration of retention of Canadian citizenship.
Section 5 (1) (a) is more or less on the same basis. This covers Canadian citizens who, for example, emigrate to the United States and their children who are minors are still considered to be citizens of Canada until their twenty first birthday is reached. They have three years of grace, but after they are 24 years old, if they do not apply for Canadian citizenship they are no longer citizens of Canada.

Bill of Rights
A large number of people emigrate from Canada to another country, raise their children there and fully intend to remain in that country. Their children may not be interested in maintaining Canadian citizenship. Why should these people continue to have the privileges of Canadian citizenship for the rest of their lives even though they are perhaps not interested in maintaining that citizenship?
It also seems to me that if this bill were passed section 6 of the Canadian Citizenship Act would not be necessary.
Then if we look at section 17 I think we have another situation which would be affected if this bill were passed. This concerns the case of dual nationality. For instance, there are a number of countries-I believe there are about 17 in Europe-such as France, Switzerland, Greece, Hungary and all the countries of the Soviet union, who consider people who have been born in their country and who have emigrated, for example to Canada, and then returned to the country of their origin, to be nationals of their country though they may have already acquired the citizenship of that other country. We could take the example of a person who has come to Canada, become a citizen, and gone back to his original country without any intention of returning to Canada. It could be that the country was at war with Canada and that this person could be fighting against Canada; yet during all that time he would have all the privileges of Canadian citizenship. It seems to me that allowing such people to retain their citizenship even in circumstances where they might be fighting against Canada would be stretching it a bit.
There is, of course, section 18 which the hon. member mentioned. I agree that if a natural born Canadian goes to another country, accepts employment and so forth, and is not required to renounce his citizenship regardless of the length of his stay in another country, then I think a naturalized Canadian should have the same privilege. I think the hon. member's point is well taken and I hope that some time in the future this section might be amended in order to grant this privilege to both types of Canadians. The hon. member mentioned the case of a person who had come to Canada and because of the nature of his work, which was highly specialized, had been obliged to leave Canada to find employment in another country where he has been living for a number of years. Section 18(1) of the citizenship act provides that a person ceases to become a Canadian citizen if he resides outside Canada for a period of ten consecutive years. Of course, there is also provision in the act for an extension of that period upon application. I think that in the case to which I have referred 
this has been done for a number of years. As the hon. member said, the case has been leniently dealt with by the department. I agree that it should be, because I think the person concerned is the type of man of whom we in Canada should be proud. I am sure he would be glad to come back to Canada if suitable employment could be found for him. I suppose similar cases could be brought to the attention of the committee.
At the same time, if we look closely at the facts of this case we find that within one month or two months of this person receiving his citizenship certificate he left the country with his family to accept employment abroad, since then he has not, to my knowledge, been back. So it appears that this type of privilege can be abused. For example, a girl who comes to Canada as a landed immigrant could marry a Canadian citizen and obtain citizenship status within a year. Then they could go abroad. She could get a divorce and under the bill now proposed still maintain her citizenship indefinitely even though she might have lived in Canada for only one year. We can see cases where abuses might arise in this regard. There is, too, the danger of abuse by foreign agents who might like the privilege of having a Canadian passport. I think we all realize that a Canadian passport is a valuable document which carries a great deal of prestige.
I have tried to point out some of these things in order to show how this bill would affect the citizenship act and why it would have been much simpler for the hon. member to have brought in his bill as an amendment to section 18 or, perhaps, some of the other sections of that act. It seems to me we are going off on a tangent when we try to amend the bill of rights. To me, the bill of rights, is a fundamental document among our Canadian statutes and one which we should regard with a great deal of respect. It is something we should try to keep as brief and as general as possible; we should not clutter it up to a point where it becomes meaningless. In this case it seems to me that the purpose of the hon. member in introducing the present bill could have been much better served by proposing an amendment to the citizenship act. In this way he could have achieved his object by a relatively minor piece of legislation rather than in the lofty manner he is trying to employ here.
In conclusion I wish to say I have no criticism at all to make of the hon. member's intentions in which he would place naturalized Canadians and natural born Canadians on the same footing. I think it is a lofty ideal.
Perhaps the hon. member would be the first to admit that under the present government a large number of the discriminations which

formerly existed in the legislation covering citizenship and immigration have been removed. It seems to me that in the old act there was a section which could have deprived a person of his citizenship after only two years abroad. I think the removal of that provision was good for the Canadian Citizenship Act.
I go along with the idea that as much discrimination as possible should be removed from the measure. There is no doubt that the act is not perfect. I am a natural born Canadian of naturalized parents and I would be the first to say that all Canadians should be placed on an equal footing. However, I think we should take care to see that we do not jeopardize the security of the country. At the same time we should do everything possible to ensure that the regulations are not a strait-jacket and that they are not such that they can be interpreted so as to discriminate against naturalized Canadians.
Perhaps at some time in the future the hon. member could reintroduce his bill as an amendment to the citizenship act. I think if he did so everyone in this house would support the lofty ideal of placing naturalized Canadians and natural born Canadians on an equal footing.

I noticed that when the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) rose to introduce this bill he said he intended to be very brief. He was very brief. He made no attempt to discuss the bill at any length nor did he try to point out the effect it would have on our citizenship laws as they now stand. Neither did he attempt to deal in any detail with the bill itself. He rose only to say that he thought the law as it stood now contained features of discrimination against persons who had come to this country and been naturalized as citizens. He was not prepared to discuss the effect on the citizenship act of the proposals he had to bring forward; he merely stood on his feet long enough to raise an emotional argument, presumably because he had no other good argument to support his proposals.
The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate specializes in emotional colour when there is nothing else to support his contentions. I was in the house when this measure came up on a previous occasion not long ago. The hon. member made a self-righteous and appealing speech in support of his argument. He was followed by a number of hon. members with some experience in this house and who know as much about this as he does. They told him that as far as they were concerned there was no merit to his amendment. But the hon. member rises today to tell us he thinks everyone in the house is ready to
Bill of Rights
accept his bill. This is one of the debating tricks of the self-righteous hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate.
It will be noticed, as was pointed out by the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Slogan), that the hon. member did not bring in his bill as an amendment to the Canadian Citizenship Act. This is not just a matter of proposing amending sections to that legislation as one would expect of an effort to change a statute. Oh no, that would be too routine for the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate. He wanted to give this special colouring of emotion and sentiment and brought in his bill as an amendment to the Canadian Bill of Rights.
We should certainly closely examine this bill before it is passed by the house. Indeed,
I feel it should never pass as an amendment to the bill of rights. The hon. member proposes sections which in my view would not appropriately form part of the bill of rights. A fundamental statute which deals with the basic rights of the Canadian people should not be cluttered up with every routine idea that is brought forward by a member of this house.
Mr. Speaker, I wonder whether the hon. member would permit a question.
By all means.

It might help him along a little, in fact. Does the hon. member consider that an assertion that all Canadian citizens are equal, which is all this bill does assert, represents a cluttering up-an odd phrase, it seems to me, sir, but that was the language the hon. gentleman used-of the bill of rights? Surely it is the most fundamental thing that could be contained in it.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentleman proposes an amendment to a statute which is now looked upon by Canadians everywhere as a sacred statement of our fundamental rights and freedoms. Actually the hon. member seeks to effect a change in the citizenship act by means of an amendment to the bill of rights. The hon. member is not prepared to argue the doubtful merits of the case, if there is any merit in seeking to effect this change. The hon. member attempts to achieve his purpose by the back door means of seeking to amend the bill of rights.
I agree with the hon. gentlemen that the equality of all Canadians is an important matter but I suggest that the citizenship act as it now stands in no way discriminates between citizens of Canada. In no way does it put one group of citizens in an unequal position.

Bill of Rights
Let us examine what is sought to be accomplished by the bill which the hon. member hopes he can sneak through before six o'clock, in one hour. What will it do?
We must first examine the means whereby Canadian citizens may be deprived of their citizenship. Under section 15 (1) of the Canadian Citizenship Act any Canadian citizen who accepts citizenship in another country automatically loses his Canadian citizenship thereby. That applies to all Canadian citizens and is, I suggest, the most usual way by which Canadian citizens lose their citizenship.
Sections 4 and 5 of the act deal with the situation in which a person may lose Canadian citizenship if he rejects the opportunity of filing a declaration of intent. A man may be born outside Canada and may never come to live here, but as a child of Canadian parents he is a Canadian citizen. These sections provide that within three years after his reaching age 21 this man will lose his Canadian citizenship unless he files a declaration to the effect that he wishes to retain it. The reference in these sections is to a man who has never lived in Canada, who was born outside the country. He is asked only to file a declaration indicating that he wishes to be considered a Canadian and retain his citizenship. The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate wishes to delete these two sections from the act so the foreign born person of Canadian parents need do nothing at all to retain his citizenship.
I submit that if a person is interested in Canada and meets the tests of citizenship, which I submit are that he wishes to live here, has some interest in the country and wishes to make some contribution to its strength, he would certainly not fail to file a declaration of his intention to remain a Canadian citizen. If a person will not do that I see no reason why he should not be deprived of citizenship. Why should the rights, privileges and immunities of Canadians be extended to those born of Canadian parents abroad, and living abroad, who reject an invitation to file a declaration indicating they wish to be considered Canadian citizens?
There is another situation in which a person may be deprived of his citizenship under the existing legislation. I refer to a man with a dual nationality, that is, born in another country, who under the laws of the country in which he was born has citizenship there even though he is now a Canadian citizen. Section 17 of the act provides that if such a man leaves Canada after becoming a citizen here, returns to the country of his origin and serves in the army of that country in a war against Canada he shall not be considered

a Canadian citizen. This is the great discrimination the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate seeks to eliminate in his selfrighteous cause this afternoon.
I see no discrimination in retaining a law that provides for the deprivation of Canadian citizenship in the case of a man with Canadian citizenship who returns to the country of his origin and serves in the armed forces of that country in a war against Canada. I see no reason why a soldier in the army of a country which is at war with Canada should have, by right, a Canadian passport, the protection of Canadian embassies and the privilege of saying he is a Canadian citizen.
Another situation in which a person may lose his citizenship is dealt with in section 18 of the act which provides that if a person who is a naturalized citizen leaves this country and resides away from it for ten consecutive years with no intention or desire to return he may lose his citizenship. This, of course, does not apply to anyone who is interested in Canada and who is abroad temporarily. The section sets out many exceptions to the general rule that a person who has been away for ten consecutive years ceases to be a Canadian citizen. If a person serves away from Canada with the armed forces, United Nations or NORAD forces then, of course, he retains Canadian citizenship. If he is absent from the country in the service of the Canadian government or of a provincial government, or represents a firm, business company or organization outside Canada, or if he is away from Canada because of ill health or disability he retains Canadian citizenship. The same applies to the spouse or minor child of any of the class of exceptions to which I have referred.
However, if he does not fall within any of these categories and has been away for ten years, in order to retain Canadian citizenship while abroad he must indicate his intention to return to Canada at some time and that his absence is for a temporary purpose. There are many naturalized Canadians who have left this country to work abroad but who intend some day to return. It is the policy of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration to extend the period in those instances as the minister has authority to do under the act. This is frequently done where a person requires an extension of absence. For all practical purposes the door remains open for such people to return to Canada and they retain their citizenship indefinitely.
There is a good reason for the inclusion of this section in the act. It is in the interests of Canada and Canadianism. Primarily it is to

prevent a person achieving Canadian citizenship who comes to Canada solely for the purpose of acquiring the prestige of Canadian citizenship status. It is to prevent a person coming here for five years, qualifying for Canadian citizenship and then taking his Canadian passport with him to wander through the rest of the world, never returning to Canada. There is no reason why Canada should extend citizenship to people with that motive solely to enjoy the privileges arising from possession of a Canadian passport. A Canadian passport is something which every one of us values. We can cheapen it by making it available to everyone who comes here only for the purpose of acquiring it and then going away, never to return but everywhere across the world in every instance representing himself as a Canadian although it might have been 40 years since he set foot on Canadian soil.
I do not think the hon. member for Bona-vista-Twillingate, if he thought carefully into the proposal he puts before us today, would really want the people of Canada to extend that type of privilege forever to someone who has no interest whatsoever in Canada except for the prestige or status which he might gain from having our passport in his pocket or from being able to say that he is a citizen of our country.
Then also there is another situation with which I am sure the hon. member for Bona-vista-Twillingate is familiar; but of course he did not refer to it because he feels that the emotional mantle of the discrimination cry alone should be sufficient to carry his argument today. I refer to the situation of a person of foreign birth who marries a Canadian and comes to Canada. After one year in Canada this person can qualify for the rights and priviliges of Canadian citizenship. After one year he or she can become a Canadian citizen. Then there is nothing to prevent that person from leaving Canada and going back to his place of origin. However, under the proposal put forward by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, this person who has spent one year in Canada is forever after that under all circumstances a citizen of Canada and is entitled to all the benefits and privileges of citizenship in this nation. I do not think he makes a reasonable argument at all when he rises to tell us that we are discriminating against this person who after living only one year in Canada, wants forever to be a Canadian citizen.
Will the hon. member permit me to ask him another question?

Of course.
Bill of Rights

Does the hon. member realize that the argument I made about discrimination was not originally made from this side of the house but rather was originally made by his own leader in the election campaign of 1957, and that what I am seeking to do is to fulfil one of the unfulfilled promises of the present leader of the government?

Since the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate has raised this matter of unfulfilled promises, a matter in which he seems to specialize, along with the emotionalism which shrouds so many of his bald arguments, may I refer for a moment to a letter which appeared in a recent issue of the Ottawa Journal and which mentioned the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate. It is dated January 22, at Sarnia, and is written by Rev. Ralph E. Bradley, United Church minister in that area. The letter reads in part as follows:
Sirs: The present campaign of Mr. Pickersgill to gain political yardage by his collection of so-called unfilled promises of Mr. Diefenbaker is hardly consistent with his past performance as a cabinet minister, and reminds us of the Pharisee who claimed to be much more righteous than his fellowmen.
I think that the argument made this afternoon by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate will appear to the rest of the members in the house to be a Pharisee type of argument. The letter goes on to say this:
If he will recall his role as superintendent general of Indian affairs and the "do-nothing" policy that he pursued while in office, he might be reminded that he issued a direct order to all members of the Indian affairs branch in Ottawa to do absolutely nothing towards solving the land question that was then developing on the Sarnia Indian reserve. He said that he would have nothing to do with it, because in his own words "it is a political hot potato".
Mr. Speaker, he is a specialist in political hot potatoes and that is what he is trying to manufacture this afternoon.

I am rising on a question of privilege, Mr. Chairman, and I am genuinely grateful to the hon. gentleman for giving me a chance to do so. I read that letter. That statement I am sure was made in good faith as it was made by a clergyman; but it is just untrue, as the hon. lady who is the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration knows very well. I approved of this sale to this New England company. It was the company itself that did not go on with the transaction. Hence the statement happens factually to be untrue. I think perhaps the gentleman who wrote the letter, in view of his profession, would have been well advised

Bill of Rights
if he had taken the trouble to ascertain what the real facts were before writing a letter of that kind.
Of course, I am not going to enter into an argument-

Since my name has entered into this discussion and since the hon. member has called me to witness with regard to his good intentions, I can only say that I certainly take his word spoken as a member of the House of Commons. However, I can scarcely be called to witness with regard to something about which I do not know.

I apologize to the hon. lady if I went further than I should have gone. We had a good deal of debate about this matter. I think she is quite right. It is not fair for me to ask her to do that. She was not minister then; I was minister at that time. It is not fair to ask her to be witness to it. However, the facts are clear and they have been put on the record many times.
Of course I do not want to enter into this argument.
I am grateful to the hon. member.

The hon. member for
Bonavista-Twillingate is better known to Mr. Bradley who had an opportunity to see the hon. member when he was minister at first hand and to understand his attitude to the Indians of the nation. I merely wish to say that Rev. Mr. Bradley concludes his letter by saying this:
-it was under Mr. Pickersgill's administration that the long inequity of our national policy to the Indian people sank to an all-time low.
I think most members of the house will agree with that statement.
On that matter I would call the hon. lady to witness because she has been following these deals ever since.

To continue, may I say that there is another situation in which a person can be deprived of citizenship. If a person who becomes a naturalized citizen of Canada commits treason against Canada or commits an offence under the Official Secrets Act and flees from Canada and will not come back to stand trial, he is then deprived of his Canadian citizenship. A person who is a traitor or a spy and hides abroad to avoid trial loses his Canadian citizenship. If the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate wishes to argue that this is discrimination, I say it is discrimination against a spy or traitor. No one else needs to worry about it.
Again I do not see why we should extend the rights of Canadian citizenship to people

who take up arms against us, who betray us, or who commit treason against us or indeed people who enter the country through fraud or misrepresentation. It is not a matter of discrimination at all. It is a matter of the people of Canada using the same rights we exercise when we pass laws to set up a method of immigration into the country.
We as citizens exercise the right to screen people who come into the country as to their suitability to mesh in with the Canadian way of life and as to their skills. We wish to inquire whether they can support themselves here. We have that right. The door is open to all who wish to come subject to this proviso, namely that they must be good citizens of Canada. Under the Canadian Citizenship Act in a few cases we reserve the right to withdraw from people, whom we once thought to be good citizens the right of Canadian citizenship if it turns out in fact that not only are they not good citizens but that they bear arms against us, spy upon us or otherwise seek to do us harm. Not only is that so, but as a matter of technical law only we withdraw citizenship from people who were born outside of Canada, who never wish to come to Canada and who have no interest in the nation, demonstrated by refusal to declare that they are Canadians.
To sum the matter up, may I say this. I think that Canadians should require from people who claim the right of citizenship in Canada that they be citizens. I noticed that the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate did not wish to argue whether or not a person who committed treason and refused to come here and stand trial should retain his citizenship. He did not wish to argue the merits of that matter. He merely stated that such a person was being discriminated against. May I say that it is not a matter of discrimination at all. It is rather a matter of the people of Canada setting up a system of rules in order to protect the value of citizenship here and abroad. It is a matter of seeing to it that people who come to this country and then desert or forsake us in order to go some place else, who wish to have no further interest in us, lose their Canadian citizenship because they are not entitled to have it. They are not citizens of Canada in fact by any manner of means. The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) wants to make them by law, what they clearly refuse to be in practice.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I regret to interrupt the hon. member but his time has expired.

Mr. Speaker, our Canadian Bill of Rights is couched in no mean language. The high principles which underlie

the history of our country are given a permanent record in our bill of rights for the bill speaks of the very highest principles and moral virtues which we can bring to bear on this important subject. The preamble speaks of the supremacy of God, the dignity of the human person and the rule of law. No acts of men can make all men free and equal. We can only do our best and in our bill of rights we have done this.
I do not want to see the bill of rights changed into a mere immigration act and I do not think that the people of Canada want this to be done. We want it to stand beside such documents as the declaration of independence of the United States and the constitution of that country. We want it to be a document which all men can always regard with reverence and respect.
I suspect that the hon. member for Bon-avista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) merely wants to bring in an amendment to this great document in order to get himself into the history books such as he is so fond of writing.
That is a reflection.

He speaks of taking away the rights of Canadian citizenship arbitrarily. I suggest that if a man who was not born here leaves our country it is an act of abdication. Far from taking away any rights from him we are restoring to him the right to belong to his own native country. I was born in Canada but I take no narrow view of this matter. Some of our finest citizens are those who have come here and made themselves equal in spiritual values and in dedication to our country. Such people we welcome. They have equality without the law. No law can make them equal because by the law of their own country they still have a status which we cannot change. We cannot be completely equal because they can abdicate their citizenship. I cannot nor do I want to, but no act of parliament can change this fact. When I have been born in Canada nothing can alter that fact.
If a man wants to leave our country and go back to the land of his birth this is something we cannot alter in any natural way, nor do I think we should do so in law by a unilateral act. Men who are born in certain countries of Europe cannot become Canadian citizens today in the eyes of their own countries and they cannot escape military service or other duties to the countries of their birth. Much as we would like to have no possible difference between our citizens in fact or in law, the fact of being born in an alien country does make a difference which we are unable to change.
If there is great disagreement with what I am saying and we wish to change the Immigration Act or the Canadian Citizenship 26207-1-34i
Bill of Rights
Act, let us do so by the proper method and in the proper statute. There is a security angle in protecting our country internally but I do not think that is the only factor involved. If we lay charges against people for treason or other acts for which they may lose their citizenship, there is a tremendous burden of proof placed upon the crown. I think this is one case where the burden of proof should be shifted to the accused to show that his own acts are not such as to indicate that he should forfeit the highest right we have, that of being a Canadian citizen.

Mr. Speaker, I have only a couple of minutes and I should like to summarize what has already been placed before us by some of the other speakers. First, while in name we have a bill which apparently is an amendment to the bill of rights it is in all respects a sweeping change in the Canadian Citizenship Act. As was shown very clearly by the hon. member for Inverness-Richmond (Mr. MacLellan), many of the provisions of that act dealing with acquisition, retention or loss of citizenship would be struck out in one blow by the bill introduced by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill). He does this under the guise of an amendment to the bill of rights and then, as has been pointed out, does not want to debate it.
Obviously we are wondering whether or not the attempt to do it in this manner means that the hon. member does not want to be drawn into a debate on those parts of the Canadian Citizenship Act which he would take out by this method. We have seen before that the politics of a situation are very important to the hon. member. I think it was demonstrated while he was a minister that he was much more interested in the politics than in the rights of the citizens involved.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. I think that what the hon. member is doing now is reflecting on my motives in bringing in this bill, which is clearly contrary to the rules. The reason the bill was introduced in this form is perfectly plain. When hon. gentlemen opposite were in the opposition they promised equality to all Canadian citizens and I am attempting to help them to keep their own promise.

I hope I have not referred to motives. I am merely suggesting that because of the way in which the hon. member is seeking to do this we are a little puzzled. If he wishes the citizenship act to be amended, then why not introduce an amendment to that act? I suggest that we have seen evidence of a little envy in the hon. member for

Business of the House
Bonavista-Twillingate because under the present government we were able to pass the bill of rights which has been welcomed by the country and is very well thought of by people generally. It is something that we have always needed and the hon. member feels that if he can get even a little amendment made to it he might be able to get some of the glory that our Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) has achieved with the bill of rights.
I would suggest that anyone who is going to consider seriously the bill which the hon. member has presented must study each one of the sections of the citizenship act which would be made ineffective by this bill.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I regret to interrupt the hon. member but it is six o'clock.
Still discriminating.

Mr. Speaker, before you leave the chair perhaps I could inquire of whoever is the acting house leader-I take it it is the Minister of National Revenue-* if, in accordance with the undertaking given by the Prime Minister when he asked to have the business interrupted, we are going back to the speech from the throne on Monday?

Mr. Speaker, I do not know about any undertaking given by the Prime Minister. I do not recall any such undertaking. At any rate, the intention is that on Monday we will deal with certain resolutions starting with No. 13 on today's order paper dealing with the Old Age Security Act. Having concluded the debate on that we shall proceed to No. 14, the one dealing with the Old Age Assistance Act. Having concluded that we shall proceed to No. 15, which is another one of the social security measures under the name of my colleague, the Minister of National Health and Welfare. Having concluded that we shall deal with No. 16. If those have been concluded we shall deal with No. 17, the measure respecting the railway in Alberta, then with No. 7 on today's order paper and then with No. 8. If by that time the house has approved all of those we shall deal with other matters on the order paper.

On a question of privilege, the hon. member questioned the undertaking given by the Prime Minister. He will find it in Hansard of January 18, at page 7, where
the Prime Minister, in asking unanimous consent to set up the committee of supply gave this undertaking, that the only matters that would be brought before the house would be those supplementary estimates. On being questioned by the Leader of the Opposition the Prime Minister said:
Might I just add this, because I want to be as fair as the Leader of the Opposition. There is also the program in connection with winter works. I do not go beyond those two.
It was on that understanding that the consent was given and I hope between now and Monday the government will consider the undertaking given by the Prime Minister.

This is in keeping with the pledge that was given. We did refer those matters to the committee of supply. The undertaking has been fulfilled and we are not referring other matters to the committee of supply.
It is sharp practice and it is shocking.
It is important that the rules of the house, as agreed upon by the committee which drafted them last year, a committee of which the hon. member was a member, be kept.

It being three minutes after six o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
